sections.html:
Allen County bills property tax for every address inside it, and the county treasurer collects. Fort Wayne is the county seat, but a house in Grabill, Huntertown, Leo-Cedarville or Monroeville gets its bill from the same county offices. The county has 20 townships and four public school districts: East Allen, Fort Wayne Community Schools, Northwest Allen and Southwest Allen.

The population was 385,410 in 2020, and about 67.6% of occupied housing units were owner-occupied.

Fort Wayne sits where three rivers meet and has a long flood history, including serious floods in 1913 and 1982. If your house is near a river or low ground, confirm its flood zone status with your insurer or the city before you list. Storm damage to a roof, siding or trees, such as the June 2012 derecho left behind, is easy to spot in an inspection, and an as-is sale means you do not have to fix it first.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax and where to pay
sections.html:
The county treasurer collects, the assessor and township assessors value property, and the auditor processes deductions. Call the treasurer's office to confirm who to ask for.

  • In person: Rousseau Centre, 1 E Main St, Suite 104, Fort Wayne, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Bring the whole statement or a reprint.
  • Kiosk: in the hallway outside the office, 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., cash and check.
  • Mail: Allen County Treasurer, PO Box 2540, Fort Wayne, IN 46801-2540.
  • Online: electronic check, credit cards, PayPal, Venmo, Apple Pay and Google Pay. Processing fees apply.
  • Phone: automated pay line at 844-576-2177.
  • Drop box: night depository on Main Street in front of the north side of the courthouse.

Spring and fall bills are mailed together in April. If yours is missing, you can print a copy from the treasurer's website.

Taxes are due in two installments, May 10 and November 10. If a due date lands on a weekend, the deadline shifts to the next business day, and the treasurer's notice shows the date. Payments must be received or postmarked by then.

When you sell, ask which installment is still open. A spring payment that was made on time can still leave a fall bill for the same year, and that bill is split between you and the buyer by closing date. Keep your payment receipts and the reprint of the bill in your closing folder. If a buyer's lender wants proof of payment, those papers answer the question quickly.

Indiana's Department of Local Government Finance sets a 5% penalty if you pay within 30 days after a due date and have no back taxes on the property. After those 30 days, or if prior taxes are unpaid, the penalty is 10%.

If you appeal an assessment, Indiana lets you pay on the previous year's assessment while the appeal is pending, without penalty.

sections.h2: How much can an Indiana tax bill rise?
sections.html:
Indiana limits what each class of property can be billed through circuit breaker caps.

Indiana circuit breaker caps by property class
Property classCap on tax as a share of assessed value
Homestead (principal residence)1%
Other residential, including buildings with two or more units2%
Agricultural land2%
Long-term care property2%
Nonresidential real property3%
Personal property3%

The 1% homestead cap applies only if the owner receives the homestead standard deduction. A house you rent out or that sits empty is generally in the 2% class instead, so the cap on an inherited house rises from 1% to 2% once homestead status ends.

sections.h2: How to appeal an Allen County assessment
sections.html:
File Form 130 with the assessing official, one petition per parcel, by June 15 of the assessment year if the county mailed the notice before May 1. When the notice is mailed on or after May 1, the deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed.

  • An informal meeting follows, where both sides trade evidence.
  • The county board (PTABOA) must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing and mail notice at least 30 days before.
  • If you still disagree, or the board does not rule in 180 days, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review.
  • Tax Court and the Indiana Supreme Court are the next levels.

The assessment is presumed correct. A recent sale of your home, comparable sales, a purchase offer or an appraisal all count as evidence. The assessor has the burden of proof if the assessment rose more than 5% over the prior date, unless the rise reflects renovation or a change of use or zoning. A missed hearing can cost a $50 penalty.

Find out which installment is open and who is paying it, then ask the title company how the current installment will be split at closing. Taxes in Indiana are billed in arrears, so a bill can come due close to your closing date.

  • Ask the title company for a payoff on the day of closing.
  • Confirm whether a lender escrow account paid the last installment.
  • Ask the assessor to review any recent value increase of more than 5%.
  • Keep the homestead deduction in mind if you move out before the sale.

Back taxes do not block a sale. The amount owed, with any penalty, comes out of your proceeds at the table. A cash buyer can close without a lender's appraisal, which helps when a tax balance and repairs are both in play, but the payoff still has to be exact. Ask the treasurer's office for the balance the week you set a closing date, and check it again just before signing so a penalty that posted in between does not surprise you.

A simple order of work helps. First, pull your latest statement or print a copy from the treasurer's website. Second, find out whether the mortgage servicer pays from escrow, since an escrow payment can mean the next installment is already covered. Third, tell the title company the date you want to close so it can prorate the installment between you and the buyer. Fourth, if you moved out and the house sits empty, ask the auditor about the homestead deduction, because a vacant house can drop into the 2% class and the bill may change.

If the house is inherited, the tax bill may still be in the name of a deceased owner. Bring the court papers to the title company early so the payoff, the deed and the sales disclosure form all carry the right names.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Allen County, Indiana?
faqs.a: They are due May 10 and November 10 each year. A payment made within 30 days after a due date carries a 5% penalty when there are no back taxes, and 10% after that.

faqs.q: How do I pay my Allen County property tax online?
faqs.a: You can pay by electronic check, credit card, PayPal, Venmo, Apple Pay or Google Pay through the treasurer's site, and processing fees apply. There is also an automated pay line at 844-576-2177.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal my Allen County assessment?
faqs.a: File Form 130 by June 15 when the county mailed the assessment notice before May 1 of the assessment year. If the notice came after May 1, the deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed.

faqs.q: How much can my Allen County property tax go up?
faqs.a: Indiana's circuit breaker caps are 1% for a homestead, 2% for other residential property and agricultural land, and 3% for nonresidential property and personal property. The homestead cap requires the homestead standard deduction.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Allen County house if I owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the treasurer or title company for the payoff, and the amount can be paid from the sale proceeds at closing. A tax balance does not stop a cash offer.
